posts.text:
Italy has been one country since 1861.

This map shows what people there actually speak — dozens of separate languages, some as distant from standard Italian as Spanish is.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ At unification in 1861, hardly anyone in Italy spoke Italian. One widely cited estimate puts it at about 2.5% of the population, with other scholars arguing for closer to 10%. Either way: the state was assembled first, the language spread afterwards.

2/ Standard Italian is essentially literary Tuscan — the language of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. A single regional variety became the national standard because of a 14th-century poet, roughly 500 years before there was an Italy to standardise.

3/ The north is a different linguistic world. Lombard, Piedmontese, Venetian, Emilian and Ligurian are Gallo-Italic — linguists group them with French and Occitan as much as with Tuscan. Mutual intelligibility with standard Italian is limited.

4/ Sardinian, the grey island, is often described as the most conservative Romance language still spoken — the closest surviving relative of everyday Latin. It is a language in its own right, not a dialect of Italian.

5/ The edges of the map are frankly foreign: German across South Tyrol, Slovenian near Trieste, French and Occitan in the Alpine valleys, Catalan in the Sardinian town of Alghero, plus Ladin and Friulian in the northeast.

6/ Then the surprises. Griko — a form of Greek — survives in small pockets of Salento and Calabria. The dark red patches are Arbëresh: Albanian-speaking villages founded by refugees from the 15th century onward, still speaking it 500 years later.

7/ Italy formally recognises twelve historic linguistic minorities under a 1999 law. Most varieties on this map have no legal status at all, and nearly all are shrinking as schooling and TV standardise speech.
